citations.desc: Consignments to carriers and intermediate handlers.
citations.narrative:
The registrant is not currently obtaining a certifying statement (e.g., “I hereby certify that the (number) primary
enclosure(s) which are used to transport the animal(s) in this shipment complies (comply) with USDA standards for
primary enclosures) from the consignor.
Not having a certifying statement such as the one above doesn't ensure that the animals being transported complies with
USDA standards for primary enclosures. The registrant must start obtaining a certifying statement such as the one above
from the consignors.
Correct by September 2, 2026.

citations.desc: Primary enclosures used to transport live animals.
citations.narrative:
During transport, one hedgehog was transported in an enclosure that had an opening on the top that did not shut tightly.
The opening could be easily slid open by people or animals. The animal escaped the enclosure during transport and was
found deceased in the vehicle two days later. Additionally, the enclosure had ventilation openings on the top of the
enclosure and did not have ventilation openings on any wall of the enclosure. The enclosure did not have projecting rims
large enough to ensure 0.75 inches of space between any adjacent cargo. No live animal markings were on the side or
top of the enclosure to ensure the correct upright position of the enclosure.
Primary enclosures used in transport that are not sufficient in structural strength may lead to animals escaping or being
injured. Animals in transport may suffocate or become heat stressed if carriers are not adequately ventilated or if
ventilation openings become obstructed. Failure to label transport enclosures could result in improper handling and
potential injury or discomfort to the animals.
The licensee must ensure that primary enclosures used to transport live animals shall be constructed in such a manner
that the structural strength of the enclosure is sufficient to contain the live animal. Primary enclosures used for transport
must have ventilation openings located on two opposite walls of the primary enclosure and the ventilation openings on
each wall shall be at least 16 percent of the total surface area of each wall, or there are ventilation openings located on all
four walls of the primary enclosure and the ventilation openings on each wall shall be at least 8 percent of the total
surface area of each wall, provided, however, that at least one-third of the total minimum area required for ventilation of
the primary enclosure shall be located on the lower one-half of the primary enclosure and at least one-third of the total
minimum area required for ventilation of the primary enclosure shall be located on the upper one-half of the primary
enclosure. Additionally, primary enclosures used to transport live animals must have a permanently affixed on top and on
one or more sides with the words "Live Animal" or "Wild Animal." These words must be 1 inch in height and have arrows
or other marking to indicate the correct upright position of the container.
Corrective actions had been implemented at the time of the inspection.

The registrant reported that while she typically has written instructions for food and water requirements for her transported
animals, she accepted sugar gliders, raccoons, and a hedgehog for transportation between July 6, 2026 and July 22,
2026 with no written instructions for the food and water requirements affixed to the outside of the primary enclosure.
Failure to have written feeding and watering instructions can result in animals who do not receive correct care during the
time of transport. The registrant must not accept any live animals for transportation in commerce unless written
instructions concerning the food and water requirements of such animals being transported is affixed to the outside of its
primary enclosure.
Correct by September 2, 2026.

According to veterinary records, two sugar gliders were delivered that had experienced distress during the shipment. One
arrived deceased, dried in parts, and decomposing, contorted in an unnatural position. The animal's body and fabric
pouch contained maggots. A sugar glider sharing the fabric pouch required medical care due to oral sores and
dehydration, but made a recovery. The transporter said she performs visual checks on the animals every four hours, but
may not observe sugar gliders due to their nature.
Not visualizing animals every four hours and not contacting a veterinarian when they are distressed or in need of care
resulted in discomfort, pain, and death.
All animals must be visually observed every 4 hours and a veterinarian must be contacted anytime an animal is showing
signs of obvious physical distress.
Correct by September 2, 2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with facility representatives.

Corrective actions had been implemented at the time of the inspection. 
3.139(e) 
   
Food and water requirements. 
The registrant reported that while she typically has written instructions for food and water requirements for her transported

3.140(a)  Critical
   
Care in transit. 
According to veterinary records, two sugar gliders were delivered that had experienced distress during the shipment. One

All animals must be visually observed every 4 hours and a veterinarian must be contacted anytime an animal is showing
